To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. Dietary K supplementation (0.5% in diet) did not prevent the development and progression of hypertension in DOA-salt rats.

Dietary potassium supplementation did not prevent the development or progression of hypertension in DOA-salt hypertensive rats and that it did not affect peripheral alpha-adrenergic but did affect peripheral beta-adrengeric responsiveness in DOCA-sal hypertensive rats.
Dietary potassium supplementation did not prevent the development or maintain the elevated blood pressure of deoxycorticosterone-salt hypertensive rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of potassium in the regulation of blood pressure.
the mechanisms by which dietary K supplementation may affect peripheral adrenergically mediated vascular responses in DOCA-saline hypertensive rats.
the role of dietary potassium in the pathophysiology of experimental hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dietary K supplementation did not alter the development of hypertension and the peripheral adrenergics responsiveness in DOCA-salts rats.

dietary potassium supplementation in the DOA-salt rat does not affect the development or the severity of hypertension, does not affect the in vitro alpha-adrenergic response of aortic smooth muscle, and only partially normalizes the in vitro beta-adrenergically mediated response of the aorta.

the effects of K supplementation on peripheral adrenergics and blood pressure in DOCA-salts are not clear cut and may be dependent on the level and/or duration of K intake and/or the level of salt intake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DOCA-saline hypertensive rat is a good model for studying the role of the sympathetic nervous system in the development of hypertension.
the DOCA-sodium model is not an appropriate model for the study of dietary potassium and blood pressure relationships in rats.
the DOCA-saline model of hypertension is not an ideal model for studying the antihypertension effect of K.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dietary potassium supplementation does not affect blood pressure in deoxycorti- coicosterone acetate-saline hypertensive rats.
the effects of K on adrenergic receptors are not the only factors that are involved in its antihypertension effects.
K supplementation does not prevent the progression of hypertension in DOCSA rats and may actually have a negative effect on blood pressure control.
